sections: # Phase 4 — the GCN encoder  (opening markdown: what the encoder computes, the [128,105,13] + [128,105,105] -> [128,105,16] shape map, and the UNTRAINED caveat in bold)
## Setup — path anchor, imports, load artefacts, load sector labels

## Check 1 — the normalised adjacency: rebuild A_hat via normalise_adjacency, assert symmetry, assert max eigenvalue is 1.0 for a connected graph, and assert the A_hat @ sqrt(deg) == sqrt(deg) eigenvector identity. Keep a short markdown note that the top eigenvector is D^1/2 * 1, the DC mode, and that it is the component which survives repeated application — oversmoothing stated in eigenvalues.
## Check 2 — layer sanity: output shapes through both layers, and a permutation-equivariance demonstration in the notebook (separate from the pytest case) showing f(PX, PAP^T) == P f(X, A)

## Check 5 — the untrained baseline embedding space  (NEW, see visuals below)

new_visual_1.section: ## Check 4 — spectral entropy and effective rank
new_visual_1.purpose: Show how many directions of the embedding space actually carry information, and how that compares to the raw features.
new_visual_1.maths_to_state_in_markdown: For singular values s_1 >= ... >= s_d of Z, define p_k = s_k / sum_j s_j. The spectral entropy is H = -sum_k p_k log p_k and the effective rank is erank(Z) = exp(H). This is a continuous count of how many dimensions are genuinely in use: a perfectly flat spectrum over d dimensions gives erank = d, and a rank-one matrix gives erank = 1. Note the hard ceiling: X has only 13 features, so Z lives in at most a 13-dimensional subspace no matter what embed_dim is set to.
figures: Figure 4a — a two-panel figure for a single mid-sample date. Left panel: the normalised singular value spectrum p_k against k, for BOTH the raw features X[t] and the embedding Z[t], on the same axes with a legend. Right panel: the cumulative sum of p_k for both, with a horizontal line at 0.9 so the reader can see how many components carry 90% of the spectral mass. Title must include the date and the word 'untrained'.

Figure 4b — effective rank across ALL 128 dates, as a time series, for both X and Z on the same axes. Add a horizontal dashed line at 13 labelled 'ceiling: n_features'. This shows whether the encoder's spectral behaviour is stable over time or varies with regime.

Figure 4c — a histogram of the per-date effective rank of Z across the 128 dates, with the mean marked. This is the 'entropy distribution' proper: it shows the spread of the effective-rank statistic rather than a single snapshot.
new_visual_1.printed_output: Mean, std, min and max of erank(Z) and erank(X) across all dates, and the date at which erank(Z) is lowest.

new_visual_2.section: ## Check 5 — the untrained baseline embedding space
new_visual_2.purpose: Show whether the graph convolution alone — before any training — already improves sector separation relative to the raw features. This is the baseline the trained encoder must beat.
new_visual_2.method: Project to 2D with PCA from sklearn.decomposition. Use PCA rather than UMAP or t-SNE: it is deterministic, adds no dependency, and its axes are interpretable as directions of maximum variance. Fit the PCA separately for X and for Z, since they live in different spaces.
figures: Figure 5a — a side-by-side scatter for a single mid-sample date. Left: PCA of the raw features X[t]. Right: PCA of the embeddings Z[t]. Both coloured by GICS sector using the same colour map and a single shared legend placed outside the axes. Annotate each panel's axis labels with the variance explained by that component. Titles must say 'untrained encoder'.

Figure 5b — the same side-by-side for a crisis date (the rebalance date nearest 2020-03-31) and a calm date (nearest 2019-06-30), so four panels in total, to show whether sector separation is regime dependent.
new_visual_2.quantitative_companion: Alongside the figures, compute silhouette_score from sklearn.metrics against the GICS sector labels, in the FULL embedding space (not the 2D projection), for both X and Z, at every date. Print the mean of each and plot both as a time series. Markdown must state plainly what this measures and what it does not: a higher silhouette for Z than for X would mean the graph convolution sharpens sector structure even at random initialisation, which would be a property of the propagation operator A_hat rather than of anything learned. State explicitly that a negative or near-zero silhouette is a normal result here and does not indicate a bug — sectors are not expected to be cleanly separated clusters in a 13-dimensional standardised feature space.
